headlines.html: On-orbit compute goes billion-dollar: Loft Orbital and Abu Dhabi's Marlan Space are investing $1 billion in a 50-satellite constellation carrying Mistral AI, analyzing imagery directly in orbit rather than downlinking it to the ground — (SpaceNews)

TrustPoint orders 40 satellites into production: LEO navigation startup TrustPoint has tapped EnduroSat US to build 40 C-band navigation satellites, moving from the demonstration phase to mass deployment — (SpaceNews)

2026-09-11.summary_html:
① Loft Orbital × Marlan Space × Mistral (SpaceNews, 9/10) — With Abu Dhabi's Royal Group putting up $1 billion, Loft Orbital and Marlan Space are expanding their AI satellite constellation, Altair, from ten to 50 satellites. The core is on-orbit compute. Instead of downlinking raw imagery to ground stations for processing, France's Mistral AI models ride aboard the satellites, analyzing directly in orbit and issuing alerts within seconds. Targets include maritime surveillance, wildfire and disaster detection, and security for ports and critical facilities. The satellites will be built by Abu Dhabi's Orbit Works, with the first launch set for October; the plan was unveiled last Tuesday at the World Space Business Week summit in Paris.

② TrustPoint × EnduroSat US (SpaceNews, 9/10) — Low-Earth-orbit positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) operator TrustPoint has ordered 40 commercial satellites from EnduroSat US. The C-band GNSS constellation will be built across three production tranches, with the first launch targeted for 2027 and full operation aimed for within the next 24 to 36 months. Following two technology-demonstration satellites in 2023 and a single full-stack demonstrator in 2025, this order marks the graduation from demonstration to commercial operations. The two developments show that the orbital-compute race is advancing beyond dedicated data-center satellites like Starcloud and SpaceX. Loft Orbital is pushing a $1 billion edge-computing model — layering AI inference onto Earth-observation satellites to "process in orbit and downlink only the conclusions" — and while it is less overt than data-center satellites, it rests on the same logic of moving computation into space. TrustPoint's 40-satellite production contract reveals the layer beneath it: the satellite mass-manufacturing capacity that any orbital-compute constellation presupposes is spreading across the US, Europe, and the Middle East. With capital from Abu Dhabi, the compute model from France, and the manufacturing line at a Bulgarian-founded US company, this deal signals that the supply chain for orbital infrastructure is already being reshaped along multinational lines.

headlines.html: Eclipse Space unveils "SurgeSat," a satellite built for orbital data centers: A satellite-platform startup founded by former SpaceX engineers announced a 100 kW-class compute satellite platform and a solar partnership with Gama — (SpaceNews / Business Wire)

FCC moves to formalize exemption of constellations from environmental review: With applications for more than one million orbital data center satellites pouring in, the agency will enshrine in rule its longstanding practice of excluding satellite constellations from environmental review — (SpaceNews)

2026-09-10.summary_html:
① Eclipse Space (SpaceNews / Business Wire, 9/9) — Eclipse Space, a satellite-manufacturing startup founded by former SpaceX engineers, emerged from stealth to unveil three satellite platforms. CitraSat targets direct-to-device (D2D) service that connects to handsets without a terminal (S-band phased array, 6 kW peak); SliceSat targets high-speed broadband (Ku-band, 8 kW); and the flagship SurgeSat is built for large-scale AI and orbital compute, pairing dual solar arrays rated at 100 kW peak power with a 400-square-meter radiator to dump heat. The model is distinctive in that customers own and operate their own constellations, and the company will co-develop a power system scalable beyond 100 kW with the solar firm Gama. It is a productization aimed squarely at power and heat rejection — the biggest bottlenecks for orbital data centers.

② FCC (SpaceNews, 9/8) — The U.S. Federal Communications Commission plans to formalize as rule its longstanding practice of exempting satellite constellations from environmental review. The decision comes as applications for more than one million orbital data center satellites flood in at an unprecedented pace, with SpaceX's orbital data center satellite concept frequently cited as a leading example. The move runs directly counter to a petition filed this past July by environmental groups including Earthjustice, which demanded a programmatic environmental impact statement (PEIS). For ODC constellations facing mass launch and deployment, it amounts to a regulatory green light that removes uncertainty from the licensing process. The two developments show that orbital data centers have moved past the "concept" stage into a phase where "products and policy" are being put in place together. On one side, newcomer manufacturers like Eclipse are diversifying the supply side by offering 100 kW-class dedicated compute satellites as catalog products; on the other, regulators are moving to remove the environmental-review uncertainty that had been an obstacle to mass deployment. The physical bottlenecks of power and heat rejection and the institutional bottlenecks of orbital congestion and the environment are being addressed at the same time. The United States is pushing the proliferation of private platforms and regulatory streamlining in parallel, while South Korea remains at the stage of trying to finalize its K-Space Data Center roadmap through a September resolution of the science and technology ministers' meeting — a gap in pace that is becoming apparent.

headlines.html: Stoke Space raises $1 billion, unveils larger fully reusable rocket: A $1 billion Series E brings its cumulative total to $2.3 billion. Alongside the fully reusable Nova, which is nearing its first orbital launch, the company announced the larger Nova Block 2, capable of lifting 15 tons to LEO — a step-change in launch capacity that carries more satellites at once — (SpaceNews)

The Exploration Company raises $450 million — the largest Series C for a European space company: The funding accelerates development of the reusable Nyx cargo vehicle and the Storm engine. Co-led by Bessemer, Atomico and the Scale Up Europe Fund, it brings the cumulative total to roughly $680 million. A major inflow of European capital into orbital logistics and transport infrastructure — (SpaceNews)

2026-09-09.summary_html:
① Stoke Space (SpaceNews, 9/8) — Stoke Space, which is developing a fully reusable launch vehicle, raised roughly $1 billion in a Series E, bringing its cumulative funding to $2.3 billion. The round was co-led by Point72 Ventures and Spark Capital, with participation from Y Combinator, Woven Capital and others. The funds will go toward the debut of Nova — the fully reusable rocket nearing its first orbital launch (slated for 2027) — and toward expanding production and launch capacity. At the same time, the company unveiled the larger Nova Block 2, capable of lifting 15 tons to LEO, which clusters 14 Zenith engines — double the number on Pioneer — with the goal of carrying more satellites at once. Orbital data centers are ultimately a business that only works if large numbers of satellites can be launched cheaply and frequently, and fully reusable heavy-lift vehicles are the step-change in launch capacity that underpins those constellations. The launch vehicle itself is not a data center, but no orbital compute constellation is possible without this transport capability.

② The Exploration Company (SpaceNews, 9/8) — The Exploration Company, a European firm developing the reusable Nyx cargo spacecraft, raised $450 million in a Series C. The largest Series C ever for a European space company, it was co-led by Bessemer Venture Partners, Atomico and EQT's Scale Up Europe Fund, with existing investors including Balderton, Plural and Cherry participating. Its cumulative funding since founding stands at roughly $680 million. The money will go toward Nyx — which will ferry cargo to commercial space stations in low Earth orbit — the reusable high-thrust Storm engine, and preliminary work on a future heavy-lift vehicle. This is not an orbital data center itself, but rather an investment in the logistics and transport layer that orbital infrastructure rides on — building up Europe's self-sufficient transport muscle for carrying people, cargo and equipment to orbit. On the same day, two of the year's largest orbital-infrastructure investments were announced side by side: America's fully reusable heavy-lift vehicle (Stoke) and Europe's reusable cargo and transport (The Exploration Company). It is a signal that capital is flowing not into orbital compute itself, but into the "plumbing" beneath it — launch and transport capacity. If last week's flows split across compute capital (Starcloud's $250 million on 8/24), launch infrastructure (SpaceX's Louisiana on 8/27), government policy (Isaacman on 8/28) and European manufacturing (IRIS² on 9/2), this week's axis is "heavy, reusable transport capability," with the U.S. and Europe bulking up simultaneously. That said, it bears emphasizing that both deals are not orbital data centers but the access and transport layer that makes them possible. Meanwhile, the roadmap for a Korean orbital data center (K-Space DC) is expected to be approved at September's ministerial meeting on science and technology, but it has not yet been finalized; if approved, it will be covered as a separate key story.

headlines.html: Pixxel raises $100 million — the largest-ever investment in an Indian space company: Pixxel, an Indian hyperspectral satellite startup, has secured $100 million in a Series C round and is expanding satellite mass-production lines in both India and the United States. It isn't an orbital data center itself, but it signals that the manufacturing base for churning out satellites at scale is spreading to a new country — (SpaceNews)

2026-09-08.summary_html: ① Pixxel Series C, $100 million (SpaceNews, 9/6) — Pixxel, a hyperspectral satellite startup based in Bengaluru, India and Los Angeles, USA, has raised $100 million in a Series C round. The round was led by Singapore's sovereign wealth fund Temasek and UK space-focused investor Seraphim, with existing investors Radical Ventures and GrowX joined by new backers 360 ONE Asset and IMM Investment, bringing cumulative funding to $195 million — the largest amount ever for an Indian space company. Pixxel already operates six of the world's highest-resolution commercial hyperspectral satellites (Firefly), and it will put this capital toward expanding its Honeybee satellite network, advancing its Aurora analytics software, scaling up manufacturing facilities in India and the US, and leading the first public-private 12-satellite Earth-observation constellation being driven by India's space agency IN-SPACe. Worth flagging — Pixxel is an Earth-observation (EO) company, not an orbital data center. But the premise of space data centers rests on an industrial base that can mass-produce satellites cheaply, and the spread of that manufacturing capacity beyond the US, China, and Europe into India is an event that widens the supply-chain and competitive landscape of the orbital-compute era. Set against the flow of the past two weeks, today's news finds its place clearly. On the US side, capital (Starcloud's $250 million), launch infrastructure (SpaceX's $100 billion Louisiana site), and the government agenda (NASA Administrator Isaacman's proposal to move compute into orbit) have been filling out the demand and policy axes of orbital compute, while Europe has been building manufacturing and launch muscle through IRIS² satellite mass production and its own launch vehicles. Pixxel adds a third dimension to this picture — a phase in which satellite manufacturing itself is no longer the preserve of a few great powers but is diffusing to emerging spacefaring nations like India. Given that orbital data centers ultimately mean constellations numbering in the tens of thousands, which country can produce satellites cheaply and quickly is the foundation of this competition — and today's news signals that the foundation has widened.

headlines.html: Europe reaches orbit under its own power: Germany's Isar Aerospace launched its Spectrum rocket from Norway's Andøya Spaceport and reached orbit. It marks the first time a commercial launch vehicle has attained orbit from continental European soil, delivering a first breakthrough on domestic launch access — the biggest bottleneck for European orbital compute — (SpaceNews)

2026-09-07.summary_html: ① Isar Aerospace Spectrum Flight 2 (SpaceNews, 9/5) — German startup Isar Aerospace launched the second Spectrum rocket from Norway's Andøya Spaceport on September 5 and successfully reached orbit. It is the first time a privately built launch vehicle lifting off from continental Europe has attained orbit. Spectrum is a small-lift rocket standing 28 meters tall with 10 engines, capable of placing up to 1 metric ton into low Earth orbit; this "Onward and Upward" mission carried six commercial and educational cubesats plus a technology-demonstration payload, and was supported by ESA's Boost! program. The maiden flight in March 2025 lost attitude control just 30 seconds after liftoff and crashed into the sea off Andøya, making this second attempt's orbital success a watershed for European NewSpace. Isar raised €270 million in a Series D that included participants such as Porsche SE, earning a valuation of roughly €2 billion and making it the most heavily capitalized independent launch company in the EU. Isar's orbital success is more than one launch company's milestone — it fills in the missing half of the European orbital compute debate. When SpaceNews warned on August 5 that "Europe's orbital compute gap is widening," and when ESA signed its first three European Launcher Challenge contracts on August 29, the underlying concern was that for Europe to place space-data-center-class infrastructure in orbit, it ultimately needs domestic launch capability that does not depend on American rockets. A small-lift rocket reaching orbit is not itself a space data center — but it is the prerequisite infrastructure that determines whether Europe can sovereignly deploy orbital compute assets in the future. While the United States forges ahead with Starcloud's fundraising and SpaceX's large-scale launch infrastructure, Europe has only now arrived at the starting line of independent orbital access. It is a signal that the orbital data center race — over capital, policy, and compute — ultimately comes down to a logistics question: who can carry it to orbit.

headlines.html: OHB Wins €1 Billion Contract to Build IRIS² Medium Earth Orbit Satellites: The SpaceRISE consortium led by SES has awarded OHB the first major contract for the EU secure connectivity network IRIS², tasking it with building 18 of the 2.6-tonne-class MEO platforms — (SpaceNews)

PLD Space Raises an Additional $125 Million — Cumulative Total Tops $550 Million: The Spanish launch company has loaded up on capital for European sovereign launch capability ahead of the first orbital flight of Miura 5 — (SpaceNews)

Northwood Space Quintuples Its Ground Station Antenna Factory: The company is opening a new 185,000-square-foot headquarters and factory in Torrance, California, shifting to mass production of hundreds of phased-array antennas per year — (SpaceNews)

2026-09-02.summary_html:
① OHB × SES (SpaceNews, 8/31) — European satellite manufacturer OHB has secured a contract worth roughly €1 billion from SES to develop and build 18 medium-earth-orbit satellite platforms for IRIS², the EU's secure satellite communications network. It is the consortium's first major contract since the program's implementation phase kicked off on August 6, with SpaceRISE — made up of SES, Eutelsat and Hispasat — handling the MEO segment. Each satellite has a launch mass of about 2.6 tonnes, and IRIS², combining low- and medium-earth orbits, comprises 348 satellites, targeting a first launch in 2029 and service start in 2030. It is not an orbital data center in itself, but rather an expansion of the industrial base as Europe pushes sovereign satellite infrastructure into a mass-manufacturing stage.

② PLD Space (SpaceNews, 9/1) — Spanish launch company PLD Space has raised an additional $125 million, bringing its cumulative funding past $550 million. The company is preparing for the first orbital launch of its small launch vehicle, Miura 5. Europe has long depended on U.S. rockets to deploy satellites because of a shortage of its own launch options, and this buildup of private launch capability shores up a precondition — low-cost, sovereign launch — for putting any future orbital computing concept into space.

③ Northwood Space (SpaceNews, 8/31) — Ground station startup Northwood Space has opened a new 185,000-square-foot headquarters and factory in Torrance, California, expanding its manufacturing floor space more than fivefold from 25,000 to 135,000 square feet. At full capacity, the phased-array portal line will turn out more than one ground station's worth of panels each month, while the parabolic prism line produces four antennas per week. Downlink throughput — bringing large volumes of orbit-computed data back to the ground — is the real bottleneck for orbital data centers, and mass-producing the ground segment is an infrastructure investment aimed squarely at widening that bottleneck. This week's signals cluster not around new compute payloads in orbit but around the industrial-base triangle that underpins them — satellite manufacturing (OHB), launch (PLD) and ground downlink (Northwood). Europe in particular is building sovereign satellite and launch capability simultaneously with IRIS² MEO manufacturing and the Miura 5 launch, yet it still has no answer to the U.S. capital-and-policy offensive in orbital computing — Starcloud's $250 million raise (8/24), SpaceX's $100 billion Louisiana launch city (8/27) and NASA Administrator Isaacman's proposal to move compute to orbit (8/28). For orbital data centers to reach economies of scale, all three legs — satellites, launch and ground stations — must thicken at once, and today's news shows all three under construction — though the contrast is stark: Europe is building infrastructure muscle, while the U.S. is scaling compute itself.
